New Deal. Franklin Delano Roosevelt's comprehensive program of federal legislation and initiatives enacted between 1933 and 1939 to address the economic crisis and social hardship of the Great Depression. It fundamentally expanded the role of the federal government through alphabet agencies and established the modern welfare state, representing a dramatic shift from laissez-faire capitalism.

The New Deal pursued three goals: Relief provided immediate aid to the poor and unemployed through the Federal Emergency Relief Administration and later the Works Progress Administration, which employed millions in public works projects. Recovery aimed at stimulating economic growth through government spending and regulation via the National Recovery Administration and the Tennessee Valley Authority managing regional economic development. Reform enacted structural changes to prevent future depressions through Social Security providing unemployment insurance, old-age pensions, and aid to the disabled, as well as the Securities and Exchange Commission regulating stock markets and the National Labor Relations Board protecting workers' right to unionize.

Major agencies included the Civilian Conservation Corps, which employed young men in conservation and public lands projects, and the Works Progress Administration, the largest relief program employing millions in public works, art, theater, and writing projects. The Tennessee Valley Authority managed hydroelectric power and economic development in the Southeast. The Social Security Act of 1935 provided old-age pensions, unemployment insurance, and aid to the disabled. The National Labor Relations Act in 1935 protected workers' right to organize and bargain collectively. The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 regulated stock markets and created the SEC.

The New Deal expanded federal power dramatically; the Supreme Court initially struck down some New Deal legislation as unconstitutional but reversed course after FDR's Court-packing threat. The Wickard v. Filburn case in 1942 greatly expanded Congress's power under the Commerce Clause. The New Deal created a permanent expansion of federal bureaucracy and welfare provisions that established the Fair Deal and later Great Society as successors to progressive reform.
